description: 65% hydration sourdough balances an easy dough with a soft, open crumb. Work out the water, starter, and salt for any flour weight, with the table.

examples.result: Add 450 g flour, 275 g water, 100 g starter, and 10 g salt. Total dough 835 g.
steps: Starter is 20% of the flour: 500 × 0.20 = 100 g.
The starter is half flour and half water, so it brings 50 g of flour and 50 g of water.
Total water is 65% of the flour: 500 × 0.65 = 325 g. Water to add is 325 - 50 = 275 g.
Flour to add is 500 - 50 = 450 g. Salt is 2%: 500 × 0.02 = 10 g.
examples.title: 500 g flour at 65% hydration

examples.result: Add 540 g flour, 330 g water, 120 g starter, and 12 g salt. Total dough 1002 g.
steps: Starter is 20% of the flour: 600 × 0.20 = 120 g.
The starter brings 60 g of flour and 60 g of water.
Total water is 65% of the flour: 600 × 0.65 = 390 g. Water to add is 390 - 60 = 330 g.
Flour to add is 600 - 60 = 540 g. Salt is 2%: 600 × 0.02 = 12 g.
examples.title: 600 g flour at 65% hydration

faqs.answer: Yes, it is one of the best starting points. The dough is soft but not sticky, it shapes easily, and the crumb is open enough to look and taste like sourdough. Many bakers settle at 65% for their everyday loaf and never leave.
faqs.question: Is 65% hydration good for a beginner?

faqs.answer: Because the starter already brings water. For 500 g of flour, 65% hydration means 325 g of water in total, and 100 g of starter brings 50 g of that water. You add the remaining 275 g. The calculator counts the starter's water so the dough lands at 65%, not above it.
faqs.question: Why is the water to add less than 65% of the flour?

faqs.answer: 65% is a good starting point for a loaf with some whole wheat, since whole wheat absorbs more water than white flour. For a loaf that is mostly whole wheat, expect to need more water still, and add it a tablespoon at a time until the dough feels soft rather than stiff.
faqs.question: Should I use 65% for a whole wheat loaf?

faqs.answer: 835 g: 450 g flour to add, 275 g water to add, 100 g starter, and 10 g salt. That makes one medium boule or one 9 by 5 inch loaf.
faqs.question: How much dough does 500 g of flour make at 65%?

faqs.answer: At 65% the dough is supple and easy to shape, with a fairly even crumb. At 70% it is softer and slacker, with a more open crumb and bigger holes, and it needs more folding to hold its shape. Five points of hydration is a real difference in handling.
faqs.question: What is the difference between 65% and 70% hydration?

felicityNote: Sixty-five percent is my Tuesday loaf. It never fights me, it slices well for school lunches, and it is the one I bake when I am not thinking about baking.

parts.meaning: Total flour in the dough, always 100% in baker's percentages. The starter's flour is part of it.
Total water as a share of total flour. At 65%, every 100 g of flour holds 65 g of water.
Starter as a share of total flour. At 20%, 500 g of flour takes 100 g of starter.
A 100% hydration starter is half flour and half water, so half its weight is flour and half is water.
Salt as a share of total flour. At 2%, 500 g of flour takes 10 g of salt.

formula.text: Starter = flour × starter %. Flour to add = flour - starter ÷ 2. Water to add = flour × hydration % - starter ÷ 2. Salt = flour × salt %.

howToSteps.name: Weigh the flour and water
howToSteps.text: Put the bowl on the scale, zero it, and weigh in the flour to add, then the water to add, holding back about 20 g of the water for now. The calculator already subtracted the starter's flour and water.

howToSteps.name: Add the starter and salt
howToSteps.text: Add the ripe starter, then the salt. Mix until no dry flour is left, then feel the dough. Add the held-back water a little at a time if the dough feels stiff.

howToSteps.name: Rest, then fold
howToSteps.text: Cover the bowl and rest for 30 minutes. Then give the dough two or three sets of stretch and folds in the first hour, folding each side up and over.

howToSteps.name: Bulk ferment and shape
howToSteps.text: Let the dough rise until it is about half as big again, domed, and jiggly, then shape it into a round or a loaf. At 65% the dough should hold its shape in the basket without spreading.

lede: At 65% hydration the dough is soft and supple but still easy to shape, which makes it the everyday workhorse of sourdough. Flour here means the total flour in the dough, including the flour inside the starter, so the hydration you ask for is the hydration you get.

name: 65% Hydration
summary: 500 g flour at 65% hydration: add 450 g flour, 275 g water, 100 g starter, 10 g salt.
title: Sourdough Calculator: 65% Hydration
tutorial: Sixty-five percent is where sourdough stops feeling like a project and starts feeling like a habit. The dough is soft enough to give you a tender crumb with some open holes, and firm enough that shaping is still straightforward. If 60% felt a little dry and 70% felt a little wild, 65% is probably your loaf.

The maths runs on baker's percentages, with flour always at 100%. For 500 g of total flour at 65% hydration, the dough holds 325 g of water in total. Your starter brings 50 g of that water, because 100 g of starter at 100% hydration is half flour and half water, so you add 275 g of water to the bowl. The starter also brings 50 g of flour, so you add 450 g of flour. Salt stays at 2%, which is 10 g.

This is also the hydration I reach for when part of the flour is whole wheat. Whole wheat absorbs more water than white flour, so a whole wheat loaf at 65% handles about like a white loaf at 60%. If your flour blend is a third whole wheat or more, 65% is a safer starting point than 60%, and you can still shape it without a fight.

The crumb at 65% sits between sandwich bread and artisan bread: even holes, a soft bite, and enough structure to hold a filling without tearing. It toasts well, it makes a proper sandwich, and it still looks like a sourdough loaf on the table. That middle ground is why so many sandwich loaves land in the 60 to 65% range.

One habit worth building at 65% is holding back a little water. Mix in all but the last 20 g or so, feel the dough, and add the rest only if it wants it. Flour changes with the season and the bag, and a dough that is slightly under-hydrated is easy to fix, while a dough that is too wet is a rescue job. The Perfect Loaf gives the same advice for every hydration: hold some back and add it only if the dough can handle it.
